questions.q: What is drift, in the Terraform sense used in this lesson?
options: The normal time it takes for a VM to finish provisioning
A Terraform provider version that is newer than the one pinned in required_providers
A delay between pushing a commit and the CI pipeline starting
When real infrastructure in the cloud no longer matches what the Terraform state file believes is there
questions.explain: Drift means reality and Terraform's recorded state have diverged, usually because something changed outside the normal Terraform workflow.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the typical real-world cause of drift?
options: Someone making an urgent fix directly in the cloud console instead of going through the pipeline
Terraform automatically changing resource configurations on its own every night
A bug in the terraform init command that corrupts the provider cache
Drift only happens when multiple people run terraform apply at the exact same second
questions.explain: The common scenario is an on-call fix made quickly in the console under pressure, leaving the state file still recording the old configuration.

questions.q: What does `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` return when it finds real differences between state and reality?
options: Exit code 1
It never returns a nonzero exit code, only a warning in the log
Exit code 0
Exit code 2
questions.explain: -detailed-exitcode returns 0 for no changes, 1 for an error, and specifically 2 when the plan detected differences — the drift signal this lesson relies on.

questions.q: Why does the drift-check workflow use `on: schedule: cron:` instead of a trigger like `on: push` or `on: pull_request`?
options: Drift can happen with no code change at all, so the check has to run on a recurring schedule regardless of whether anything was pushed
cron triggers are required for every GitHub Actions workflow to be valid
schedule triggers run faster than push triggers
pull_request triggers are not supported for Terraform workflows
questions.explain: Since drift comes from changes made outside the repository entirely, a push- or PR-based trigger would never catch it — only a recurring schedule check will.

questions.q: Once drift is detected, what does this lesson say should happen next?
options: Immediately delete the drifted resource with terraform destroy
Ignore it, since -detailed-exitcode automatically fixes the mismatch
Wait for the next scheduled check to see if it resolves itself
Deliberately either codify the manual change into the configuration, or apply to put the resource back the way the config describes
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that the mismatch should never just be left — either update the .tf files to match the real change on purpose, or apply to restore the configured state.
